reason: The hypothesis makes specific mechanistic claims about surface segregation, chemical ordering, and their effect on melting in a specific HEA nanoparticle system, but cites no prior evidence whatsoever to support these premises. Standard textbook knowledge does not cover the detailed behavior of this complex five-component nanoscale system, so the lack of cited support leaves all key premises ungrounded.
premises: Element-specific surface energy and diffusivity differences drive local chemical ordering and surface segregation during cooling.
Greater surface segregation lowers the effective energy barrier for melting, broadening and lowering the melting transition.
Uniform chemical distribution maintains a higher and more abrupt melting point.
Synthesis route (cooling rate) can control the degree of chemical uniformity versus surface segregation in Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles.
Nanoscale phase-transition behavior in chemically complex nanoparticles is governed by local atomic arrangements rather than bulk thermodynamics.
